prompt: An office adds a second router, hq2, on the same LAN as hq and changes nothing else. Why does that not protect the office when hq dies?

choices.text: hq2 needs a reboot to notice
choices.why: hq2 has nothing to notice: nobody sends it anything.

choices.text: Hosts only use their one gateway
choices.why: Right. default via 192.168.10.1, and hq2 is not 192.168.10.1.

choices.text: Two routers on one LAN cause a loop
choices.why: Routers on one LAN are ordinary; loops are a switching problem, lesson 20 of networks-addressing.

choices.text: The ISP only accepts traffic from hq
choices.why: hq2 has its own link and address at the ISP, 203.0.113.3.

prompt: Several VRRP groups can share one LAN because each has its own number, the ___, which is 10 in this lab.
Match each line of hq's keepalived.conf to what it does.
hint: One of them is about the other link.

pairs.right: Names the group on this LAN
Gives up the address if the ISP link fails

prompt: hq2's log says it became MASTER at 18:10:58 and BACKUP again at 18:10:59. Why was it master for that second?

choices.text: It started first, so its wait ran out first
choices.why: Right. A second later hq's wait ran out too, and 150 beat 100.

choices.text: hq was misconfigured for that second
choices.why: Nothing in hq's file changed; only time passed.

choices.text: A lower priority wins the first election
choices.why: Priority always favours the higher number; hq2 won because nobody else was talking yet.

choices.text: The laptop chose hq2 by sending to it first
choices.why: Hosts take no part in the election.

prompt: A backup with priority 100 and an advertisement interval of 1 s waits three intervals plus (256 − priority)/256 s. How many seconds is that, to two decimals?
Where do the master's VRRP advertisements go?
hint: tcpdump on the laptop saw them.

choices.text: To hq2's own address, 192.168.10.3
choices.why: They are not addressed to one router; any number of backups may be listening.

choices.text: To the ISP router
choices.why: They stay on the LAN they protect.

choices.text: A multicast group, 224.0.0.18
choices.why: Right. Which is why the laptop could capture them too.

choices.text: 192.168.10.1, the virtual address
choices.why: The master holds that address; sending to it would be talking to itself.

prompt: The advertisements say authtype none, so a host on the LAN could claim the gateway with a higher priority. What is the defence this lesson recommends?

choices.text: Set a VRRP password in the configuration
choices.why: It travels in clear on the same LAN, which is why version 3 dropped it.

choices.text: Give hq the highest priority, 255
choices.why: An intruder can send 255 too, and a tie is settled by address, not by trust.

choices.text: Advertise faster than any intruder
choices.why: The interval says nothing about who sent an advertisement.

choices.text: Keep untrusted hosts off that segment
choices.why: Right. A VLAN of their own, or switch filters that accept VRRP only from the routers' ports.

prompt: The laptop's ARP entry for 192.168.10.1 shows 52:54:00:a8:0a:02. What is that address?
hint: Compare it with the MAC VRRP's standard asks for.

choices.text: hq's own hardware address, its real MAC
choices.why: Right. keepalived's default mode answers with the real MAC; use_vmac is not set.

choices.text: VRRP's virtual MAC for group 10
choices.why: That would be 00:00:5e:00:01:0a.

choices.text: The laptop's own MAC
choices.why: The laptop's ends in :14.

choices.text: A MAC shared by hq and hq2
choices.why: hq2 has its own, :03, and the entry changes to it after the failover.

prompt: A LAN has three backups with priorities 200, 150 and 100, all hearing the same master. The master dies. Which one takes over, and why that one?

choices.text: The 100: lowest priority acts first
choices.why: Its skew is the longest, 156/256 of a second, so it speaks last.

choices.text: Whichever booted first
choices.why: Start order mattered at start-up, when nobody was master; here all three were waiting.

choices.text: The 200, whose skew is the shortest of the three
choices.why: Right. It speaks first, and the other two hear a higher priority and stay backups.

choices.text: All three, until a vote is taken
choices.why: VRRP has no vote; the timers make one of them first.

prompt: Reply 13 arrived at 1790629866.652789 and reply 29 at 1790629869.916964. How long was the gap, in seconds, to three decimals?
hq2's master down interval is about 3.61 s, yet the ping measured a gap of 3.264 s. Why is the gap shorter?

choices.text: keepalived rounds the interval down to whole seconds
choices.why: The log prints whole seconds; the timer does not run in them.

choices.text: hq2 had been counting since hq's last advertisement
choices.why: Right. That advertisement left up to a second before the cable came out.

choices.text: The laptop's ping ran faster during the failure
choices.why: The pings went out every 0.2 s throughout; only the replies stopped.

choices.text: hq told hq2 it was leaving
choices.why: Its LAN cable was out: nothing hq sent could reach hq2.

prompt: How can we tell that none of the 3.264 seconds was delay in the network?

choices.text: The ping printed no errors
choices.why: It printed fifteen lines of no answer; that is not the evidence.

choices.text: Failover times are the same on every network
choices.why: They depend on the timers and on when the master died.

choices.text: Every reply took under half a millisecond
choices.why: Right. 0.078 to 0.493 ms: one computer talking to itself. The gap is VRRP waiting.

choices.text: The laptop and web1 share a switch
choices.why: They do not; web1 is in the data centre, two routers away.

prompt: After the failover, what had changed on the laptop?

choices.text: Its default gateway became 192.168.10.3
choices.why: The gateway address stays .1; that is the whole idea.

choices.text: The MAC it holds for .1, now hq2's
choices.why: Right. :02 became :03, and the laptop did nothing to cause it.

choices.text: Its own IP address
choices.why: The laptop is still 192.168.10.20.

choices.text: Nothing: VRRP is invisible to hosts
choices.why: The address is the same, but in keepalived's default mode the MAC behind it is not.

prompt: hq broadcast `Request who-has 192.168.10.1 tell 192.168.10.1` twice when it took over. What is that packet for?
hint: Nobody is meant to answer it.

choices.text: Checking that nobody else uses .1
choices.why: hq2 did hold .1 moments before, and the packet is not waiting for its reply.

choices.text: Asking the laptop for its MAC
choices.why: It asks about 192.168.10.1, not about the laptop.

choices.text: Repointing hosts' ARP entries
choices.why: Right. A gratuitous ARP: hosts update the entry to the sender's hardware address.

choices.text: A VRRP advertisement in ARP form
choices.why: Advertisements go to 224.0.0.18 as VRRP; this is plain ARP.

prompt: Put hq's log lines from this lesson in order.
hint: Its afternoon: in charge, cable out, cable back, in charge.
items: Entering FAULT STATE, when its LAN cable comes out
Entering BACKUP STATE, when the cable is back
Entering MASTER STATE, four seconds later
trap: A returning router comes back as a backup first; it takes over only after listening.

prompt: Suppose track_interface had been left out and hq's ISP link fails while its LAN cable is fine. What does the office see?

choices.text: No internet at all
choices.why: Right. hq keeps advertising 150 on eth0 and keeps an address it can do nothing with, while hq2 waits with a working link.

choices.text: A normal failover to hq2 after about 3.6 s
choices.why: hq2 takes over only on silence, and hq is still advertising.

choices.text: Traffic shared between both routers
choices.why: Only the master forwards for the virtual address.

choices.text: Slower internet through the LAN
choices.why: There is no slower path through hq; it has no way out at all.

prompt: What does preemption cost the office when the failed router comes back?

choices.text: Nothing, because the return is instant
choices.why: It is short, not free; this lab did not measure it.

choices.text: A second, shorter switch-over
choices.why: Right. Worth it if the returning router is better, and not if the two are equal.

choices.text: The office loses its gateway until someone intervenes
choices.why: Preemption is automatic; nobody needs to intervene.

choices.text: hq2 goes into FAULT and must be restarted
choices.why: hq2 simply returns to BACKUP when it hears a higher priority.

prompt: In this lesson, which events made hq give up 192.168.10.1? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look for FAULT in its log.

choices.text: Its LAN cable was pulled
choices.why: Right. FAULT at 18:11:06.

choices.text: Its ISP link, eth1, went down
choices.why: Right. Netlink reports eth1 down, then FAULT, at 18:11:16.

choices.text: hq2 sent a higher priority
choices.why: hq2's priority is 100, below hq's 150.

choices.text: The laptop's ARP entry went STALE
choices.why: A host's cache has no say in the election.

prompt: What are HSRP's default timers?

choices.text: Advertisement every 1 s, dead after about 3.6 s
choices.why: Those are VRRP's, as this lesson measured.

choices.text: Hello every 3 s, dead after 10 s
choices.why: Right. A gap of around ten seconds when nobody has tuned them.

choices.text: Hello every 10 s, dead after 30 s
choices.why: Slower than HSRP's defaults by a factor of three.

choices.text: None: it reacts to link state
choices.why: A dead router on a working link changes no link state; hellos are needed.

prompt: A host's ARP table shows 0000.0c07.ac0a for its default gateway. What does that tell you?
hint: The last two hex digits are a group.

choices.text: VRRP group 10, in keepalived's default mode
choices.why: keepalived's default mode shows the router's real MAC, and VRRP's virtual one starts 00-00-5E.

choices.text: The gateway is a GLBP forwarder
choices.why: GLBP hands out MACs of its own form, one per forwarder.

choices.text: The gateway is HSRP group 10
choices.why: Right. 0000.0c07.ac followed by the group in hex; 0a is 10.

choices.text: The gateway's cable is faulty
choices.why: A MAC says who owns an address, not how healthy a cable is.

prompt: What does GLBP do that one VRRP group cannot?

choices.text: Fail over faster, with sub-second hellos by default
choices.why: Its defaults are HSRP's, 3 s and 10 s, slower than VRRP's.

choices.text: Authenticate the routers to each other
choices.why: Load sharing is what sets it apart, not authentication.

choices.text: Give each host a different gateway address
choices.why: That is the two-group trick; GLBP keeps one address for everyone.

choices.text: Spread hosts across routers under one address
choices.why: Right. The ARP answer differs per host, a different virtual MAC each time.

prompt: A call centre's phones drop a call after two seconds of silence. The gateway pair runs keepalived with the settings of this lesson. Will calls survive a gateway failure?
hint: Compare the measured gap with two seconds.

choices.text: Yes, VRRP is designed for voice
choices.why: It was designed for gateways; the timers decide what survives.

choices.text: No: this lesson measured 3.264 s
choices.why: Right. And the gap ranges up to about 3.6 s; they need sub-second timers.

choices.text: Yes, if the phones use TCP
choices.why: Voice is carried on UDP, and retransmitting speech three seconds late does not help a conversation.

choices.text: Only if preemption is switched off
choices.why: Preemption governs the return, not the failure itself.

prompt: hq is master. Its LAN side is fine, its ISP link is dead, and the office has no internet although hq2 is healthy. Which single change makes the office recover on its own next time?

choices.text: A shorter advert_int
choices.why: hq would only advertise its uselessness more often.

choices.text: use_vmac on both routers, so hosts keep one MAC
choices.why: That changes the MAC hosts learn, not who is master.

choices.text: Tracking the ISP interface on hq
choices.why: Right. track_interface eth1 puts hq in FAULT, and hq2 takes the address, as this lesson showed.

choices.text: nopreempt on hq2
choices.why: hq2 is not the one that needs to change its mind.
